headline: Strait of Hormuz Crisis Drives WTI Above $100 as Canada Posts 0.1% GDP Growth and 84,000 Job Losses
executive_summary:
The Strait of Hormuz closure drove WTI crude above $100 for the first time since July 2022 — the disruption, which has restricted an estimated 20 million barrels per day of seaborne oil flows since approximately March 2,104 pushed WTI to US$102.88/bbl on March 30 and Brent to US$112.78/bbl, a record 55% monthly gain since the contract’s 1988 inception.104 The Dallas Federal Reserve estimated a one-quarter closure could reduce global GDP growth by 2.9 percentage points in Q2 2026.108 The project database tracks 63 oil and gas projects and 785 power and energy projects across Canada; Alberta accounts for 727 of these tracked projects.

The energy price surge arrived alongside the weakest Canadian labour market reading since the pandemic — employment fell by 84,000 (-0.4%) in February, reversing Q4 2025 gains, with full-time positions down 108,000 and private-sector employment down 73,000.144 The unemployment rate rose to 6.7%, up 0.2 percentage points from January.144 Services-producing industries lost 56,000 positions; goods-producing industries lost 28,000, with wholesale and retail trade recording the largest sectoral decline at 18,000 jobs.144 The database tracks 1,034 projects currently under construction that depend on labour availability and cost conditions.

GDP growth held positive at 0.1% in January while the Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at 2.25% — the second consecutive monthly GDP increase was led by a 1.2% expansion in mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction, offsetting a 1.4% contraction in manufacturing.149 The advance estimate indicates 0.2% growth in February.149 Headline CPI fell to 1.8% year-over-year in February — the lowest since early 2021 — with core measures converging near 2.3–2.4%.145 The BoC cited weaker near-term growth from US tariffs as the primary factor for holding rates steady on March 18.67

Trade data underscored the divergence between energy strength and broader economic softness — the merchandise trade deficit widened to $3.6 billion in January from $1.3 billion in December, as motor vehicle and parts exports dropped 21.2% to $5.4 billion while energy exports rose 4.1%.143 The April 2 trade data release covers the first full month of the Hormuz closure. Statistics Canada releases the March Labour Force Survey on April 3.150 The Bank of Canada delivers its next rate decision on April 15, alongside the Monetary Policy Report and March CPI data.69

The ECB rate sits 25bp below the BoC’s 2.25% — the euro strengthened to 1.1460 EUR/USD on March 31.114 Germany’s contraction reduces demand for Canadian resource exports under the CETA framework.

The BoE rate exceeds the BoC’s by 150bp — UK-Canada trade operates under the CPTPP framework. The Hormuz crisis has elevated energy import costs for the UK, a net energy importer.

financialMarkets.summary:
The BoC held at 2.25% on March 18, its seventh consecutive hold after seven cuts from 5.00% — bond markets priced 86% probability of no change at April 15.6768 The 2-year yield stood at 2.95%, the 10-year at 3.58%, producing a 2–10 spread of 63bp.

WTI surged above $100 for the first time since July 2022 — settling at US$102.88/bbl (+50% in March) as the Hormuz closure disrupted ~20M bbl/day of seaborne flows.104 Brent hit US$112.78/bbl, recording its largest monthly gain since 1988.104 Gold fell ~14% to ~US$4,578/oz, the steepest monthly drop since October 2008.44

The Canadian dollar weakened 1.85% M/M to 0.7198 CAD/USD — reflecting the 125–150bp spread between the Fed’s 3.50–3.75% and the BoC’s 2.25%.58 The TSX closed at 32,427, up 1.54% on the day but down ~6% for March (+28.2% YoY).59 The S&P 500 rallied 2.40% on March 31 on US-Iran talk reports, but remains ~9.4% below its January peak.61

financialMarkets.commentary:
WTI crude settled at US$102.88/bbl on March 31 — its first weekly close above $100 since July 2022 — as the Strait of Hormuz closure disrupted an estimated 20 million barrels per day of seaborne oil flows.131 Brent rose to US$112.78/bbl, recording its largest monthly gain since contract inception in 1988.131 The TSX Composite closed at 32,427, gaining 1.54% on March 31 while declining approximately 6% over the full month.133 Gold fell to approximately US$4,578/oz — down 14% from a March 3 peak of US$5,161/oz — while the Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at 2.25%.134135

The cross-reference engine links 63 oil and gas projects to the current WTI price environment, with 727 Alberta projects carrying direct commodity exposure.136 The 364 mining projects in the database hold exposure to gold's 14% monthly decline. The Government of Canada yield curve held a normal shape with the 2-year/10-year spread at 63 basis points, covering 1,034 under-construction projects in the database.138
financialMarkets.equityNarrative:
The S&P/TSX Composite closed at 32,427 on March 31, up 1.54% on the session but down ~6% for March — the index posted a 28.2% YoY gain despite Hormuz-driven volatility.59 Energy was the top-performing sector as WTI surged above $100; materials and financials lagged.59

The S&P 500 rallied 2.40% on March 31 on reports of US-Iran diplomatic talks — the Nasdaq gained 3.24% and the Dow ~2.0% on the session.61103 The S&P 500 remains ~9.4% below its January 2026 peak.61
financialMarkets.fxNarrative: The Canadian dollar closed at 0.7198 USD/CAD on March 31, declining 1.85% month-over-month to a two-month low as geopolitical uncertainty drove safe-haven demand for the US dollar.146 The USD/CAD rate moved to 1.3893, reflecting a widening differential between the Bank of Canada's overnight rate of 2.25% and the US Federal Reserve's target rate of 4.25-4.50% — a spread of approximately 200-225 basis points favoring the US dollar.147148 The euro strengthened to 1.1460 against the US dollar as European markets repriced geopolitical risk premiums; this EUR/USD level reflects a divergence between the ECB's rate path and US monetary policy expectations.149 If the CAD/USD rate holds near 0.72, the database's 49 export-exposed manufacturing projects would face elevated input cost pressure from US dollar-denominated material costs, while energy exporters would see higher CAD-denominated revenues from US-dollar-priced crude.150
financialMarkets.yieldNarrative: The Government of Canada yield curve maintained a normal (upward-sloping) shape through the week of March 24-30, with the 2-year/10-year spread at 63 basis points — wider than the 60 basis point spread recorded a year ago.151 The 2-year yield closed at 2.95%, up 33 basis points from 2.62% a year ago, while the 10-year yield closed at 3.58%, up 36 basis points from 3.22% a year ago, reflecting higher term premiums associated with elevated federal government debt issuance and geopolitical uncertainty.152 The 30-year yield closed at 3.94%, up 41 basis points from 3.53% a year ago. If the current long-end yield environment persists, the database's 1,034 under-construction projects — which depend on long-term financing rates for project completion — would face funding costs at the higher end of their feasibility study assumptions.153

marketCommentary:
WTI crude settled at US$102.88/bbl on March 31 — its first weekly close above $100 since July 2022 — as the Strait of Hormuz closure disrupted an estimated 20 million barrels per day of seaborne oil flows.131 Brent rose to US$112.78/bbl, recording its largest monthly gain since contract inception in 1988.131 The TSX Composite closed at 32,427, gaining 1.54% on March 31 while declining approximately 6% over the full month.133 Gold fell to approximately US$4,578/oz — down 14% from a March 3 peak of US$5,161/oz — while the Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at 2.25%.134135

The cross-reference engine links 63 oil and gas projects to the current WTI price environment, with 727 Alberta projects carrying direct commodity exposure.136 The 364 mining projects in the database hold exposure to gold's 14% monthly decline. The Government of Canada yield curve held a normal shape with the 2-year/10-year spread at 63 basis points, covering 1,034 under-construction projects in the database.138

equities.name: TSX Composite
equities.commentary: The TSX Composite closed at 32,427 on March 31, gaining 1.54% on the day as reports of potential US-Iran negotiations drove energy and risk-sensitive sectors higher.139 The index declined approximately 6% over the full month of March, reflecting elevated uncertainty from Middle East supply disruption and the February employment loss of 84,000 jobs.140 Energy sub-indices posted the largest monthly gains within the TSX, consistent with WTI crude's advance above $100/bbl, while materials underperformed amid gold's 14% monthly decline. The database tracks 727 Alberta projects — the province most directly exposed to TSX energy sector performance — and 364 mining projects with direct materials sector linkage.141

equities.name: S&P 500
equities.commentary: The S&P 500 closed at approximately 6,496 on March 31, rising 2.40% on the day, though the index remained approximately 9.4% below its January 2026 peak on a closing basis.142 March was characterized by elevated volatility driven by Middle East geopolitical developments and the Strait of Hormuz supply disruption; the March 31 advance followed reports that the US government is considering diplomatic resolution to the Iranian standoff.143

equities.name: DJIA
equities.commentary: The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at approximately 46,117 on March 31, advancing approximately 2.0% on the day alongside the broader US market rally.144 Blue-chip industrials with Canadian supply chain exposure — including steel and energy equipment names — tracked the energy sector's advance as WTI moved above $100/bbl.

equities.name: Nasdaq Composite
equities.commentary: The Nasdaq Composite closed at approximately 21,469 on March 31, the largest percentage advance among major US indices at 3.24% on the day.145 Technology-linked names outperformed on the expectation that diplomatic resolution of the Hormuz crisis would reduce input cost pressure on data centre and grid electrification projects; the database tracks 18 telecom and data infrastructure projects in Canada with US market linkages.

fx.fx_commentary: The Canadian dollar closed at 0.7198 USD/CAD on March 31, declining 1.85% month-over-month to a two-month low as geopolitical uncertainty drove safe-haven demand for the US dollar.146 The USD/CAD rate moved to 1.3893, reflecting a widening differential between the Bank of Canada's overnight rate of 2.25% and the US Federal Reserve's target rate of 4.25-4.50% — a spread of approximately 200-225 basis points favoring the US dollar.147148 The euro strengthened to 1.1460 against the US dollar as European markets repriced geopolitical risk premiums; this EUR/USD level reflects a divergence between the ECB's rate path and US monetary policy expectations.149 If the CAD/USD rate holds near 0.72, the database's 49 export-exposed manufacturing projects would face elevated input cost pressure from US dollar-denominated material costs, while energy exporters would see higher CAD-denominated revenues from US-dollar-priced crude.150

yieldCurve.yield_commentary: The Government of Canada yield curve maintained a normal (upward-sloping) shape through the week of March 24-30, with the 2-year/10-year spread at 63 basis points — wider than the 60 basis point spread recorded a year ago.151 The 2-year yield closed at 2.95%, up 33 basis points from 2.62% a year ago, while the 10-year yield closed at 3.58%, up 36 basis points from 3.22% a year ago, reflecting higher term premiums associated with elevated federal government debt issuance and geopolitical uncertainty.152 The 30-year yield closed at 3.94%, up 41 basis points from 3.53% a year ago. If the current long-end yield environment persists, the database's 1,034 under-construction projects — which depend on long-term financing rates for project completion — would face funding costs at the higher end of their feasibility study assumptions.153

commodityCommentary: The Strait of Hormuz closure drove WTI crude above $100/bbl for the first time since July 2022, producing the most significant commodity repricing event of the current cycle and placing the database's 63 oil and gas projects directly in scope.154 Energy dominated March commodity performance, with WTI gaining more than 50% month-over-month and Brent recording its largest monthly gain since contract inception in 1988. Gold recorded its steepest monthly decline since October 2008 — down 14% from a peak of US$5,161/oz on March 3 to US$4,578 by month-end — as margin liquidation and US dollar strength overwhelmed safe-haven demand.155 Base metals were mixed, with copper holding its range and nickel declining, while agricultural commodities remained broadly stable. The database tracks 364 mining projects with direct commodity price exposure.156
wcsAnalysis: The Western Canadian Select differential narrowed to approximately US$2.50/bbl below WTI as of March 27, compared to the 12-month average of approximately US$9.95/bbl. The narrow differential reflects elevated North American refinery demand for non-Hormuz crude during the supply disruption, which reduces the typical pricing disadvantage for Canadian heavy oil producers. The TMX pipeline, operational since May 2024, provides Alberta producers with Pacific Coast access at 890,000 b/d capacity, supporting crude export alternatives independent of the Gulf Coast market.157

commoditiesFull.name: Western Canadian Select (WCS)
commoditiesFull.commentary: WCS traded at approximately US$97.14/bbl on March 27, reflecting a narrow US$2.50 differential below WTI compared to the 12-month average differential of approximately US$9.95/bbl.157 The narrow discount reflects elevated North American demand for non-Hormuz crude; Alberta oil sands producers with TMX pipeline access to Pacific Coast markets benefit from an additional export option.

commoditiesFull.name: Brent Crude
commoditiesFull.commentary: Brent crude closed at US$112.78/bbl on March 31, recording its largest monthly percentage gain since contract inception in 1988 as the Hormuz supply disruption affected a greater share of Brent-priced flows.154 The Brent-WTI spread of approximately US$9.90 reflects the differential impact of the disruption on international versus North American crude benchmarks.

commoditiesFull.name: Natural Gas (Henry Hub)
commoditiesFull.commentary: Henry Hub natural gas prices held at approximately US$3.05/MMBtu in late March, with the EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook projecting an average of US$3.80/MMBtu for 2026.158 AECO prices remained elevated on global supply tightness; BC LNG project economics and Alberta gas production operations are tracked through the oil and gas project segment of the database.

commoditiesFull.name: Gold
commoditiesFull.commentary: Gold declined to approximately US$4,578/oz by month-end, its steepest monthly drop since October 2008, falling from a peak of US$5,161/oz on March 3 as margin calls and US dollar strength drove sellers.155 The 364 mining projects in the database include concentrations in British Columbia, Ontario, and Quebec, where gold mine expansion economics are sensitive to sustained price levels.

commoditiesFull.name: Silver
commoditiesFull.commentary: Silver traded at approximately US$73.33/oz as of March 25, declining month-over-month alongside gold as precious metals broadly repriced in the second half of March.159 Ontario and British Columbia silver-bearing mining projects in the database share exposure to the broader precious metals price environment.

commoditiesFull.name: Copper
commoditiesFull.commentary: Copper traded in a US$5.25 to US$6.01/lb range through March, with mixed signals from China PMI recovery and US tariff uncertainty preventing a clear directional move.160 British Columbia copper mining projects — the largest cluster of copper-linked projects in the database — and grid electrification projects with copper input cost exposure are tracked in the mining and power/energy sectors.

commoditiesFull.name: Uranium (URA ETF / CCO.TO)
commoditiesFull.commentary: The URA ETF uranium proxy closed at US$46.86, declining 2.8% week-over-week and 17.0% month-over-month alongside broader risk-off sentiment in metals, while Cameco (CCO.TO) closed at C$147.75, down 14.1% month-over-month.161 Saskatchewan uranium operations — including Cameco's McArthur River and Cigar Lake mines — represent the primary North American uranium production base; physical uranium spot prices (approximately US$92/lb) remain above the $65-70 mine operating cost range cited in Cameco's annual filings.

commoditiesFull.name: Nickel
commoditiesFull.commentary: LME nickel traded at approximately US$14,641/MT in late March, declining month-over-month amid weak demand signals from battery supply chain markets.162 Ontario and Manitoba nickel projects — including the Vale Voisey's Bay processing expansion and Sudbury operations — and battery supply chain projects in the database carry exposure to nickel price levels.

commoditiesFull.name: Wheat
commoditiesFull.commentary: Wheat futures held at approximately 607.5 cents per bushel ($6.075/bu) in mid-to-late March, with prices stable following earlier seasonal adjustments.163 Prairie grain storage and handling infrastructure projects in the database are tracked under the agriculture sector; wheat prices at current levels are consistent with the feasibility economics of grain terminal expansion projects tracked in Saskatchewan and Manitoba.

commoditiesFull.name: Canola
commoditiesFull.commentary: Canola futures traded at approximately C$633/MT in late March, reflecting stable Prairie oilseed demand and refinery consumption.164 Saskatchewan and Manitoba canola crushing capacity projects tracked in the database depend on the sustained margin between canola and canola oil/meal prices; the current level is broadly consistent with reported crush margin feasibility thresholds.

commoditiesFull.name: Potash (Nutrien NTR proxy)
commoditiesFull.commentary: Nutrien (NTR.TO) closed at C$104.62, down 1.0% week-over-week and up 1.0% month-over-month, as a proxy for Saskatchewan potash mine operating conditions.165 Mosaic and Nutrien's Saskatchewan operations — tracked in the database under the mining sector — represent the world's largest potash-producing basin; muriate of potash (MOP) spot prices of approximately US$455/MT are consistent with the economics reported in recent expansion announcements.
